Root
root
n. (the part of a plant that fixes and feeds it; figuratively, origin and source; rendering Hebrew shoresh, Greek rhiza)
From Old Norse rot, cognate with the Latin radix. In Scripture the root is always the hidden and determining part — what feeds the visible tree and what an axe is laid to when the tree is to be ended.

Biblical Definition

A root in Scripture is the hidden source that determines the visible thing, and it is used most strikingly of Christ. Isaiah prophesies from a felled dynasty: “there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots” (Isaiah 11:1) — a stem is what is left when a tree has been cut down, and the Messiah comes not from the standing house of David but from its stump. The servant song develops it: “he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness” (Isaiah 53:2). Nothing about the soil or the shoot promised anything. Revelation then reverses the genealogy in a single clause: “I am the root and the offspring of David” (Revelation 22:16) — he is David's descendant according to the flesh and David's source according to his deity, which is exactly the puzzle he put to the Pharisees about how David could call his son Lord. Paul uses the word for a moral origin: “the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows” (1 Timothy 6:10). The verse is commonly misquoted as though money were the root; the text says the love of it, and names two consequences — erring from the faith, and self-inflicted grief.

Webster 1828 Definition

The hidden part that fixes and feeds. Messiah comes as a shoot from a felled stump and a root out of dry ground, and calls himself both the root and the offspring of David; the love of money is named the root of all evil.

expand to see more

ROOT, n. [Sw. rot; L. radix.] That part of a plant which enters and fixes itself in the earth, and serves to support the plant in an erect position.

2. The part of any thing that resembles the roots of a plant in manner of growth.

3. The origin or cause of any thing; that from which a thing proceeds; as, the love of money is the root of all evil.

4. The bottom or lower part of any thing; as the root of a mountain.

5. A race; a family; descendants; as, the root of Jesse, Is. 11.

Key Scripture

Isaiah 11:1 — "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots:"

Isaiah 53:2 — "For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, there is no beauty that we should desire him."

1 Timothy 6:10 — "For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows."

Revelation 22:16 — "I Jesus have sent mine angel to testify unto you these things in the churches. I am the root and the offspring of David, and the bright and morning star."

Modern Corruption

1 Timothy 6:10 is misquoted to condemn money itself, which lets the actual sin escape — and the root is treated as the visible symptom rather than the hidden appetite Paul names.

expand to see more

The popular form of the verse — money is the root of all evil — is not what Paul wrote, and the difference matters in both directions. It lets a poor man think himself safe when covetousness is fully available to those who have nothing, and it lets a rich man think himself condemned when Scripture nowhere forbids wealth as such: Abraham was rich, Job was restored to more than he had, and Paul in the same chapter instructs the rich rather than dismissing them, charging them to trust in the living God rather than in uncertain riches and to be rich in good works. The condemned thing is the love, an appetite that operates equally at every income, and its symptoms are erring from the faith and piercing oneself through with many sorrows — both self-administered.

The principle to recover is Isaiah's stump. The house of David was cut down; the throne was empty and the family reduced to a carpenter in a village. From that stem comes the rod, and from those roots the Branch, so that the very hopelessness of the wood is part of the sign. Isaiah 53 says the same of the man — a root out of a dry ground, with no form or comeliness that anyone should desire him. God's way of bringing his greatest work out of what looks finished and unpromising is not an occasional exception in Scripture; it is his settled manner, and it should govern how a Christian reads the state of his own soil.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew shoresh is a root, and by extension a bottom or origin; geza is the stem or stump of a felled tree. Greek rhiza is a root, used of Christ and of the love of money.

expand to see more

Hebrew shoresh (H8328) — a root; also the origin or lowest part of a thing.

Hebrew geza (H1503) — a stock or stump of a felled tree; the stem of Jesse, Isaiah 11:1.

Hebrew netser (H5342) — a shoot, a branch; the rod that comes out of the stem.

Greek rhiza (G4491) — a root; the root of David, and the root of all evil.

Greek philarguria (G5365) — love of money, avarice; the actual root named in 1 Timothy 6:10.

Usage

"Of Messiah from a felled house: a Branch shall grow out of his roots (Isaiah 11:1)."

"Of the unpromising soil: as a root out of a dry ground (Isaiah 53:2)."

"Of the hidden moral origin: the love of money is the root of all evil (1 Timothy 6:10)."
